title: How do banks make money, and what matters in a banking case?
description: Retail banking economics for case interviews: net interest margin, fees, cost-to-income ratio, branches versus digital, and credit risk, with a worked…
hook: A bank makes money mainly by borrowing cheaply (customer deposits) and lending at a higher rate, then adding fees for accounts, cards, payments and advice. What matters in a banking case is how wide that interest spread is, how efficiently the bank runs, how many loans go bad, and how much equity it must hold against the risks it takes.
body:
How banks make money

  • Net interest income (NII): interest earned on loans minus interest paid on deposits and other funding. For most retail banks this is the biggest line.
  • Fees and commissions: account fees, card interchange (a small cut of each card payment), payments, foreign exchange, wealth management and advice.

Against that income sit three kinds of cost: operating costs (staff, branches, IT, compliance), credit losses (loans that are not repaid) and the cost of capital. Regulators require banks to fund a minimum share of their risky assets with equity rather than deposits, so every new loan ties up shareholders' money that expects a return.

The measures that matter

MeasureFormulaWhat it tells you
Net interest marginNII ÷ interest-earning assetsHow profitable the lending spread is
Cost-to-income ratioOperating costs ÷ total incomeHow efficiently the bank runs
Cost of riskCredit losses ÷ loansHow much of the loan book goes bad
Return on equityNet profit ÷ equityWhether the bank beats its cost of capital

A worked example: one simple bank, top to bottom

An illustrative lender has $1B of loans earning 7%, funded by $900M of deposits paying 3% and $100M of equity. It also earns $7M a year of fees.

  • Interest income: $1B × 7% = $70M. Interest expense: $900M × 3% = $27M.
  • Net interest income: $70M − $27M = $43M, a net interest margin of 4.3%.
  • Total income: $43M + $7M fees = $50M.
  • Operating costs: $20M, so the cost-to-income ratio is $20M ÷ $50M = 40%.
  • Credit losses: 1.5% of loans = $15M.
  • Pre-tax profit: $50M − $20M − $15M = $15M. After 25% tax, net profit is $11.25M, a return on equity of 11.25%.

Notice that $43M of net interest income became $11.25M of profit. Always keep interest income, net interest income and net profit separate.

Now interest rates fall. Loan rates drop from 7% to 6%, but deposit rates are already low and barely move. Interest income falls to $60M, NII to $33M, a 23% drop in the bank's main income line from a one-point rate change. Going the other way, raising the deposit rate by 0.5 percentage points to keep savers costs $900M × 0.5% = $4.5M a year, 30% of pre-tax profit. That is why rate moves and deposit pricing are such common case triggers.

Why growing the loan book is not automatically good

Lending more lifts revenue now. If the bank grows by lowering its credit standards, the losses tend to arrive a year or two later, long after the revenue has been booked. The right test is risk-adjusted return: does the extra lending earn more than the equity it ties up, after expected losses? The second practice question below works through one.

Typical banking case questions

  • How can we cut operating costs by 15%? (branches, call centres, IT; see the cost reduction guide)
  • Our digital bank is adding customers fast but losses are growing. Why?
  • Why have mortgage applications fallen?
  • Should we buy a fintech, or build the product ourselves? (a build, partner or buy question)

What a strong answer sounds like

Weak: "To grow profit, the bank should lend more."
Strong: "More lending only helps if the new loans earn more than their funding cost, expected losses and the equity they tie up. I'd want the loss rate and pricing for the new segment before recommending growth."

Common mistakes

  • Calling net interest income profit. Operating costs, credit losses and tax all come after it.
  • Ignoring the funding side. A bank can lose margin because deposit rates rose, not because loan rates fell.
  • Forgetting capital. Two loans with the same margin can have very different returns if one needs much more equity behind it.
  • Treating customer numbers as success. For a digital bank, a customer with an empty account costs money to acquire and serve. Ask about balances and card spend per customer (unit economics).

Practise

1. A bank has $5B of loans at 6% and $4.5B of deposits at 2.5%. What is its net interest income and its margin on loans?

Show the answer

Interest income: $5B × 6% = $300M. Interest expense: $4.5B × 2.5% = $112.5M. NII = $187.5M. Margin: $187.5M ÷ $5B = 3.75%.

2. The bank in the worked example (return on equity 11.25%) could add $200M of loans to riskier borrowers at 8%, with expected losses of 4% a year. It would fund them with $180M of new deposits at 3% and $20M of new equity. Ignoring extra operating costs and at 25% tax, should it?

Show the answer

Extra interest: $200M × 8% = $16M. Extra funding cost: $180M × 3% = $5.4M. Expected losses: $200M × 4% = $8M. Pre-tax gain: $16M − $5.4M − $8M = $2.6M, or $1.95M after tax. Return on the new equity: $1.95M ÷ $20M = 9.75%, below the bank's current 11.25%. On these numbers it dilutes returns, and any extra operating cost makes it worse.

3. An app-only bank signed up 60% more customers than last year, but its losses doubled. What would you look at first?

Show the answer

Revenue per customer (deposit balances, card spend, products held), acquisition cost per customer, cost to serve, and credit losses on any lending. The likely story is many low-balance customers who cost more to win and serve than they earn. Then segment: which customer groups are profitable?

Where to practise next

Try the Lumen Bank case on a fast-growing digital bank with rising losses, the Lattice Payments case on buying a fintech, and the Larchwood Bank case on valuing an AI tool for developers. The glossary entry on cost of capital explains the return hurdle in plain English.
